1. Introduction
A prominent approach to efficiently solving convex optimization problems is to reduce them to solv-
ing a sequence of linear systems. For example, interior point methods reduce linear programming,
semidefinite programming, many empirical risk minimization problems, and more to essentially
solving a sequence of ℓ2 (or least-squares) regression problems or, more broadly, to a sequence
of linear systems (Karmarkar, 1984; Lee et al., 2019; Nesterov and Nemirovskii, 1994; Renegar,
1988; Wright, 1997). More recently, improvements in quasi-self-concordant (Bach, 2010; Carmon
et al., 2020b; Karimireddy et al., 2018) and high-order (Bullins, 2020; Nesterov and Polyak, 2006;
Nesterov, 2021) optimization have yielded new ways of using linear system solvers for solving
well-established machine learning problems, including ℓ∞ and logistic regression.
    Similarly, recent advances in iterative refinement have shown how to reduce ℓp -regression, a
natural data analysis problem, to solving a sequence of linear systems (Adil et al., 2019, 2024).
ℓp regression problems appear in a wide range of applications, including semi-supervised learn-
ing (Alamgir and Luxburg, 2011; Flores et al., 2022; Kyng et al., 2015), data clustering and learn-
ing (Elmoataz et al., 2015, 2017), and low-rank matrix approximations (Chierichetti et al., 2017).
    In this paper, we study a natural generalization: rather than reducing to ℓ2 -regression, i.e.,

Future work and open problems. This paper provides improved rates for multiple convex op-
timization problems by using non-Euclidean optimization. However, these new rates come with
costs. Whereas ℓ2 -regression can be solved by matrix multiplication and linear system solving,
smoothed ℓp -regression is a more general and potentially complex optimization problem. Conse-
quently, implementing steps of our algorithm efficiently and using this to obtain end-to-end runtime
improvements for structured optimization problems is an interesting direction for future research.
     Additionally, though we settle the complexity of convex optimization with the ℓsp (λ)-proximal
oracle, this does not necessarily imply that our reduction from ℓs to smoothed ℓp -regression is opti-
mal. Consider, for example, solving ℓ6 -regression using ℓ2 -regression and compare it with solving
ℓ6 -regression via ℓ4 -regression. Our results state that the former would use ≈ n1/4 iterations of solv-
ing least squares regression, while the iteration complexity of the latter would improve to ≈ n1/13
(improving upon ≈ n1/10 iteration complexity due to Adil and Sachdeva (2020)), each of which
would involve solving an ℓ4 -regression problem. Curiously, if we further solve each ℓ4 -regression
problem using ℓ2 -regression, we would require n1/5 such problems at each step, leading to a total

2. Warm-up: Conceptual Proximal Point with Line Search
In this section, we analyze a simpler version of our generalized proximal point algorithm. Our aim is
first to provide clarity for the convergence rates, while in the following section we address the issue
of overall computational cost. Specifically, in this section we present an algorithm where each iter-

on Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration (Monteiro and Svaiter, 2013). These implicit problems can be
solved using an additional line-search procedure as in previous works (e.g., (Monteiro and Svaiter,
